title: Soft Sensing of Melt Index in Multi-Grade Polyethylene Production: Benchmarking against the Last-Laboratory-Value Baseline
abstract: Soft sensors that estimate the melt index of polyethylene online are proposed to replace delayed laboratory results, but to be useful they must beat the simplest baseline. On the public sequential-reactor multi-grade (SRMG) industrial data (331 samples, four grades; research use only, after Liu, Gao and Chen, 2013) we compared ridge regression, random forest and just-in-time (nearest-neighbour) learning with a baseline that repeats the last laboratory value of the same grade, using one-step-ahead rolling-origin evaluation over the last 166 samples. The final melt index of the third reactor had a mean of 0.104 and a standard deviation of 0.078. The baseline had a root-mean-square error of 0.0426 (R² 0.32); just-in-time learning reached 0.0412 (R² 0.37), random forest 0.0441 and ridge regression 0.171. The difference between just-in-time learning and the baseline was -0.0088 to +0.0118 (95% block-bootstrap interval), so it cannot be distinguished from zero. At the 14 samples that began a grade transition the baseline error rose to 0.106 and ridge regression had the lowest error (0.079), random forest (0.106) was no better than the baseline and just-in-time learning was in between (0.088). The sample is small and comes from one process, and the transition result rests on 14 points, so the conclusion is limited: no soft sensor clearly beat the baseline over all samples, and grade transitions are the only place where a model improved on it.

Abstract

Soft sensors that estimate the melt index of polyethylene online are proposed to replace delayed laboratory results, but to be useful they must beat the simplest baseline. On the public sequential-reactor multi-grade (SRMG) industrial data (331 samples, four grades; research use only, after Liu, Gao and Chen, 2013) we compared ridge regression, random forest and just-in-time (nearest-neighbour) learning with a baseline that repeats the last laboratory value of the same grade, using one-step-ahead rolling-origin evaluation over the last 166 samples. The final melt index of the third reactor had a mean of 0.104 and a standard deviation of 0.078. The baseline had a root-mean-square error of 0.0426 (R² 0.32); just-in-time learning reached 0.0412 (R² 0.37), random forest 0.0441 and ridge regression 0.171. The difference between just-in-time learning and the baseline was -0.0088 to +0.0118 (95% block-bootstrap interval), so it cannot be distinguished from zero. At the 14 samples that began a grade transition the baseline error rose to 0.106 and ridge regression had the lowest error (0.079), random forest (0.106) was no better than the baseline and just-in-time learning was in between (0.088). The sample is small and comes from one process, and the transition result rests on 14 points, so the conclusion is limited: no soft sensor clearly beat the baseline over all samples, and grade transitions are the only place where a model improved on it.
Keywords: soft sensor; melt index; polyethylene; grade transition; benchmark
1. Introduction

In polymer plants the melt index of the product is measured in the laboratory, with a delay of hours, while the plant is operated continuously. A soft sensor estimates the melt index from process variables, and its use is most attractive where it matters most, when the grade is changed and the off-specification product made during the transition is wasted (Kadlec et al., 2009; Fortuna et al., 2007). Many soft sensors have been proposed for multi-grade polyethylene, and each is compared with other models in its own paper.

A comparison with the simplest alternative is often missing. A plant that has a laboratory result for the grade it is running already has an estimate of the next result: the last laboratory value of the same grade. A soft sensor is worth deploying only if it is better than this value, in particular during transitions, where the last value of the same grade is out of date by construction.

This paper makes that comparison on the public SRMG data set, which was published for academic use together with a soft-sensor study (Liu et al., 2013). It contributes (i) a rolling-origin benchmark of three standard model families against the last-value baseline, (ii) a separate analysis of the samples that begin a grade transition, and (iii) an interval for the difference between the best model and the baseline, which shows how far the data can support a claim of improvement.
2. Related work

Reviews of data-driven soft sensors in the process industry list linear regression, partial least squares, neural networks and just-in-time or local learning as the main families, and point to the difficulty of changing process conditions (Kadlec et al., 2009). Just-in-time learning builds a local model for each query from the most similar past samples and is a standard answer to multi-grade operation (Cheng and Chiu, 2004). The SRMG data set was introduced in a study on sequential-reactor multi-grade processes (Liu et al., 2013).

Rolling-origin evaluation, in which the model is refitted at each step and tested on the next observation, is a standard way to test forecasts on ordered data without leakage from the future (Tashman, 2000). We use it here because the samples are ordered in time.
3. Data

The SRMG data set holds 331 samples from a polyethylene line with three sequential reactors: 12 input variables for the first reactor, 8 for the second and 9 for the third, the laboratory melt index of each reactor (MI1, MI2, MI3), and a grade number. The inputs in the file are scaled; the melt index values are as given. There are four grades with 45 samples for grade 7001, 3 samples for grade 7003, 72 samples for grade 7501, 211 samples for grade 8001. The target is MI3, the melt index of the final product, which has a mean of 0.104 and a standard deviation of 0.078. The data are public for academic research and are not redistributed here.
4. Method

Task. Samples are taken in the order of the file. For each sample t in the second half (samples 166 to 331), models are fitted on samples 1 to t-1 and predict MI3 of sample t. The inputs are all process variables of the three reactors and the laboratory values MI1 and MI2 of the upstream reactors; MI3 itself is never an input.

Models. Ridge regression with the penalty chosen from 13 values between 0.001 and 1000 by cross-validation on the training samples; a random forest of 100 trees; and just-in-time learning as distance-weighted regression on the 10 nearest samples. The baseline repeats the last MI3 of the same grade, and the previous sample when the grade has not occurred before. A second baseline repeats the previous sample whatever its grade.

Measures. We report the root-mean-square error (RMSE), R² and mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) over the 166 test samples, separately for the 14 samples that begin a grade transition (the grade differs from that of the previous sample) and for the rest. The difference between the RMSE of a model and that of the baseline is given with a 95% interval from a moving-block bootstrap (blocks of 5 samples, 5,000 resamples).
5. Results

Over all 166 test samples the last-value baseline had an RMSE of 0.0426 and an R² of 0.32 (Table 1). Just-in-time learning was slightly better (0.0412, R² 0.37), the random forest slightly worse (0.0441), and ridge regression much worse (0.171). The baseline that ignores the grade was worse than the baseline that uses it (0.0515).
Table 1. One-step-ahead results on the last 166 samples (14 of them begin a grade transition).

The differences from the baseline were small compared with their uncertainty. For just-in-time learning the difference in RMSE was -0.0088 to +0.0118, for the random forest -0.0069 to +0.0162, and for ridge regression +0.0019 to +0.2404; the first two intervals include zero.

At the 14 transition samples the baseline was poor (0.106, R² -0.06). Ridge regression had the lowest error (0.079, R² 0.40), just-in-time learning 0.088, and the random forest 0.106, which is no better than the baseline. At steady samples the baseline (0.0310) was as good as the forest and the nearest-neighbour model, and ridge regression was far worse (0.177).
6. Discussion and limitations

The main finding is a negative one: over all samples no soft sensor clearly beat the last laboratory value of the same grade. This does not show that soft sensors are useless; the baseline benefits from a data set in which 122 of the 166 test samples belong to one grade and 152 of them follow a sample of the same grade, where the last value is a strong predictor.

The only place where a model clearly improved on the baseline was the transition, and there ridge regression, the model that was worst overall, was the best. This is consistent with the idea that a linear model extrapolates across grades while local models and trees stay close to the training samples of the grade they know. With 14 points we do not claim it as a result, only as a hypothesis that a larger data set with more transitions could test.

Limits of the study. The data come from one process and 331 samples, with one grade of only three samples. The test set has 14 transition samples, so the transition result has a wide uncertainty, which we did not quantify further. The inputs are scaled and their physical meaning was not used. The models were not tuned beyond the ridge penalty. The comparison uses one-step-ahead prediction with the laboratory value of the previous sample available to the baseline, which is the situation of a plant with regular laboratory sampling and not of one with long gaps. No economic measure such as the waste made during a transition was computed.
7. Conclusion

On the public SRMG data, a baseline that repeats the last laboratory melt index of the same grade (RMSE 0.0426) was matched by just-in-time learning (0.0412, difference -0.0088 to +0.0118) and beaten only at grade transitions, where ridge regression had the lowest error (0.079 against 0.106) on 14 points. A soft-sensor proposal for multi-grade polyethylene should therefore report its error against this baseline and show its advantage on transitions with more data.
Implementation and reproducibility

The benchmark is the module research/srmg_benchmark of the product repository (data loading, rolling-origin fitting of the three models and the baselines, metrics and the block bootstrap), with three unit tests on synthetic data that check the logic; they are not used for any reported result. Every number in Table 1 and in the text is written by research/srmg_benchmark/run.py to results.json. The repository documents the maturity level of its components (TRL 4, synthetic data); this benchmark adds a measurement on public plant data but does not change that level, and the product's sequencing function is not part of the paper.
Data and code availability
The SRMG data set is public for academic research (Liu et al., 2013) and is not redistributed. The analysis code and result files are in the author's private repository and are available on request.
